claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) transmit extracellular signals to the inside by activation of intracellular effector proteins.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) transmit extracellular signals to the inside by activation of intracellular effector proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in GPCR biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Different agonists can promote differential receptor-induced signaling responses, termed bias.
source: Different agonists can promote differential receptor-induced signaling responses – termed bias – potentially by eliciting different levels of recruitment of effector proteins.
evidence: This is a known concept in GPCR pharmacology supported by the scientific literature.

claim: Bias is potentially caused by different agonists eliciting different levels of recruitment of effector proteins.
source: Different agonists can promote differential receptor-induced signaling responses – termed bias – potentially by eliciting different levels of recruitment of effector proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism of bias.

claim: The study compared the efficacy of seven agonists to induce G protein, GRK2, and arrestin3 binding to the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor using FRET-based assays.
source: Here, we compared the efficacy of seven agonists to induce G protein, G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2), as well as arrestin3 binding to the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M3 by utilizing FRET-based assays.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: GRK2 binding was studied in the presence of inhibitors of Gi and Gq proteins to avoid interference between G protein activation and GRK2 recruitment.
source: In order to avoid interference between these interactions, we studied GRK2 binding in the presence of inhibitors of Gi and Gq proteins
evidence: This describes the experimental design to isolate GRK2 recruitment from G protein effects.

claim: Arrestin3 binding was analyzed to prestimulated M3 receptors to avoid differences in receptor phosphorylation influencing arrestin recruitment.
source: analyzed arrestin3 binding to prestimulated M3 receptors to avoid differences in receptor phosphorylation influencing arrestin recruitment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for phosphorylation differences.

claim: Substantial differences were measured in the agonist efficacies to induce M3R-arrestin3 versus M3R-GRK2 interaction.
source: We measured substantial differences in the agonist efficacies to induce M3R-arrestin3 versus M3R-GRK2 interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rank order of the agonists for G protein- and GRK2-M3R interaction was the same.
source: However, the rank order of the agonists for G protein- and GRK2-M3R interaction was the same
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: G protein and GRK2 binding to M3R requires similar receptor conformations.
source: suggesting that G protein and GRK2 binding to M3R requires similar receptor conformations
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that G protein and GRK2 recruitment have the same rank order.

claim: Requirements for arrestin3 binding to M3R are distinct from those for G protein and GRK2 binding.
source: whereas requirements for arrestin3 binding to M3R are distinct.
evidence: This is an inference from the different rank orders observed for arrestin3 versus G protein/GRK2 recruitment.

claim: GPCRs can sense a wide variety of different agents, from single photons in the case of rhodopsin to small proteins that activate chemokine receptors.
source: GPCRs can sense a wide variety of different agents, from single photons in the case of rhodopsin to small proteins that activate chemokine receptors (Shichida and Imai, 1998; Griffith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An agonist binding to the orthosteric pocket increases the population of active receptor conformations.
source: an agonist, increasing the population of active receptor conformations, binds to the orthosteric pocket
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR activation mechanisms.

claim: Agonist binding leads to a conformational change of the transmembrane helix bundle that results in an opening of the intracellular effector-binding cavity.
source: this leads to a further conformational change of the transmembrane helix bundle that results in an opening of the intracellular effector-binding cavity
evidence: This describes the structural mechanism of GPCR activation, which is established knowledge.

claim: G proteins bind to the intracellular pocket of the receptors and are thereby activated.
source: G proteins bind to the intracellular pocket of the receptors, are thereby activated and enabled to transmit and modulate a multitude of signals
evidence: This is established knowledge about G protein activation by GPCRs.

claim: G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) are recruited to the activated receptors, leading to receptor phosphorylation.
source: G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) are recruited to the activated receptors, leading to receptor phosphorylation
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of GRKs in GPCR signaling.

claim: Arrestins bind to the active conformation of receptors after being activated by an initial binding to phosphorylated residues at the intracellular end of the receptors.
source: arrestins bind to the active conformation of these receptors after being activated by an initial binding to phosphorylated residues at the intracellular end of the receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about arrestin recruitment to GPCRs.

claim: Arrestins induce internalization and desensitization of the receptors.
source: Subsequently, arrestins induce internalization and desensitization of the receptors (Ritter and Hall, 2009; Martí-Solano et al., 2016; Scheerer and Sommer, 2017; Kenakin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Different agonists can stabilize distinct receptor conformations and thereby influence the recruitment of effector proteins leading to 'functional selectivity' or 'ligand bias'.
source: There is strong evidence that different agonists can stabilize distinct receptor conformations and thereby influence the recruitment of effector proteins leading to 'functional selectivity' or, more specifically, 'ligand bias' to better reflect the nomenclature in the upcoming BJP guidelines (Costa-Neto et al., 2016; Martí-Solano et al., 2016; Wingler et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019; Kenakin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Receptor conformations exist that are preferentially recognized by either arrestins or G proteins.
source: It has been shown before that receptor conformations exist that are preferentially recognized by either arrestins or G proteins.
evidence: This refers to previous findings in the literature.

claim: Agonist-dependent recruitment of GRK2 to an opioid receptor exists.
source: The recent study of Stoeber et al., 2020 has shown that agonist-dependent recruitment of GRK2 to an opioid receptor exists.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Functional bias at the level of arrestin recruitment is affected by both receptor recruitment rates of GRKs and arrestins.
source: This leads to the question whether a functional bias at the level of arrestin recruitment (Carr et al., 2016) is affected by both receptor recruitment rates of GRKs and arrestins.
evidence: This is a question posed based on previous findings, representing speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Receptor stimulation with 30 µM ACh resulted in a reversible increase in YFP fluorescence and a corresponding decrease in mTurq fluorescence, reflecting FRET development due to Gq, GRK2, or arrestin3 binding to the M3R.
source: As expected, receptor stimulation with 30 µM ACh resulted in a reversible increase in YFP fluorescence and a corresponding decrease in mTurq fluorescence, reflecting the FRET development due to Gq, GRK2, or arrestin3 binding to the M3R, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes experimental observations from FRET measurements shown in a figure.

claim: For many receptors including M3R, signal amplification at the level of G protein activation leads to a spare receptor phenomenon.
source: For many receptors including M3R, it is well known that signal amplification at the level of G protein activation leads to a spare receptor phenomenon
evidence: This is established knowledge in GPCR pharmacology.

claim: The spare receptor phenomenon allows only indirect determination of agonist efficacy by means of comparing concentration-response curves with those of ligand binding.
source: which allows only indirect determination of agonist efficacy by means of comparing of concentration-response curves with those of ligand binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations in measuring agonist efficacy.

claim: The efficacy ranking for Gq recruitment to M3R is: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are≈Guva>Pilo>Mda.
source: Our results showed the highest recruitment of Gq for ACh, followed by Metha and Fur (∼60% of the ACh signal), and much weaker recruitment for Guva and Are (∼20%) followed by even lower values for Pilo and Mda (∼8%) (Figure 1B), leading to the following ranking in efficacy: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are≈Guva>Pilo>Mda.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ranking in potency for Gq activation measured by BRET is: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are>Guva>Pilo>Mda.
source: We also performed bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based assays to study Gq activation by these agonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), with the following similar ranking in potency: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are>Guva>Pilo>Mda.
evidence: This is a primary finding from BRET experiments shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The rank order of agonist affinity determined by radioligand displacement assays is: Pilo>ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are>Guva»Mda.
source: In addition, radioligand displacement assays were performed (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) in order to determine the rank order of agonist affinity: Pilo>ACh>Metha≈Fur>Are>Guva»Mda.
evidence: This is a primary finding from radioligand displacement experiments shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Mda failed to displace the radioligand at concentrations up to 100 mM, indicating a very low affinity for the orthosteric binding pocket of M3R or a noncompetitive binding mode.
source: Mda failed to displace the radioligand at concentrations up to 100 mM, indicating a very low affinity for the orthosteric binding pocket of M3R or – despite its structural similarity to ACh – a noncompetitive binding mode.
evidence: This is an inference from the radioligand displacement data.

claim: The rank order of the efficacy of different agonists to recruit GRK2 to M3R was the same as determined for Gq recruitment.
source: The rank order of the efficacy of the different agonists to recruit GRK2 to M3R, determined by single-cell FRET assays, was the same as determined for Gq recruitment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B in comparison with Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: When Gq activation was completely abolished by pretreatment with FR900359, no recruitment of GRK2 to M3R was observed in cells transfected with Gq and fluorescently labeled M3R and GRK2.
source: Indeed, when Gq activation was completely abolished by pretreatment with FR900359, no recruitment of GRK2 to M3R was observed in cells transfected with Gq and fluorescently labeled M3R and GRK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FRET measurements shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Preincubation with PTX completely abolished agonist-evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2.
source: Likewise, preincubation with PTX completely abolished agonist-evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FRET measurements shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Without overexpression of Gαq proteins, preincubation with PTX and FR900359 pretreatment did not lead to a full inhibition of agonist evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2, presumably due to bystander FRET upon G protein-independent translocation of GRK2 to M3R.
source: Interestingly, without overexpression of Gαq proteins, preincubation with PTX and FR900359 pretreatment did not lead to a full inhibition of agonist evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), presumably due to bystander FRET upon G protein-independent translocation of GRK2 to M3R.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with a speculative explanation for the mechanism.

claim: Kinetic analysis of agonist-evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2 with or without pretreatment with PTX and FR900359 showed fast one-phased decays for signals measured with pretreatment and slower two-phased decays for signals measured without pretreatment.
source: Kinetic analysis of agonist-evoked FRET between Gβγ and GRK2 with or without pretreatment with PTX and FR900359 showed fast one-phased decays for signals measured with pretreatment and slower two-phased decays for signals measured without pretreatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A CAAX-box was introduced at the C-terminus of GRK2-YFP to allow for G protein-independent plasma membrane localization of GRK2.
source: In order to abolish the possible involvement of Gβγ and Gαq proteins in the recruitment process of GRK2 to M3R (Wolters et al., 2015) further, we aimed to bypass Gq-dependent translocation of GRK2 to the plasma membrane by introducing a CAAX-box at the C-terminus of GRK2-YFP to allow for G protein-independent plasma membrane localization of GRK2 (Inglese et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes an experimental design strategy supported by citations.

claim: D110 was mutated to alanine in GRK2, which attenuates Gαq binding to GRK2.
source: In addition, we mutated D110 to alanine, which attenuates Gαq binding to GRK2 (Wolters et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes an experimental design strategy supported by a citation.

claim: Under conditions of complete Gq and Gi inhibition, amplitudes of agonist-evoked FRET increases were reduced and offset kinetics after agonist withdrawal were substantially faster for (D110A)GRK2-CAAX compared to wild-type GRK2.
source: Under conditions of complete Gq and Gi inhibition (see for control Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), amplitudes of agonist-evoked FRET increases were reduced and offset kinetics after agonist withdrawal were substantially faster (compare Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data across different conditions.

claim: Agonist-specific interactions between (D110A)GRK2-CAAX and M3R were still measurable under conditions of complete G protein inhibition.
source: However, we were still able to measure agonist-specific interactions between (D110A)GRK2-CAAX and M3R (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FRET measurements shown in figures.

claim: The relative efficacy ranking of agonists to recruit (D110A)GRK2-CAAX without the influence of G proteins is: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Guva≈Are>Pilo.
source: Our measurements of the relative efficacy of the agonists to recruit this GRK2 construct without the influence of G proteins resulted in the following ranking: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Guva≈Are>Pilo (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mda did not lead to detectable responses in (D110A)GRK2-CAAX recruitment.
source: Mda did not lead to detectable responses.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the GRK2 recruitment assay.

claim: The relative responses induced by weak partial agonists were substantially reduced in G protein-independent GRK2 recruitment compared to G protein-dependent recruitment of GRK2, but the rank order of the agonists was essentially unchanged.
source: Even though the relative responses induced by the weak partial agonists were substantially reduced compared to the G protein-dependent recruitment of GRK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), the rank order of the agonists was essentially unchanged.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data across different conditions.

claim: The color switch of the attached fluorophores had no effect on the relative agonist efficacies for GRK2 recruitment.
source: We ensured that the color switch of the attached fluorophores had no effect on the relative agonist efficacies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Control experiments without overexpression of Gαq showed a similar efficacy of the partial agonists Pilo and Are for GRK2 binding to M3R compared to those measured under complete G protein inhibition with the G protein-insensitive GRK2.
source: Control experiments without overexpression of Gαq, but in the context of non-mutated fluorescent GRK2, showed a similar efficacy of the partial agonists Pilo and Are for GRK2 binding to M3R compared to those measured under complete G protein inhibition with the G protein-insensitive GRK2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Overexpression of Gq proteins leads to an enhanced affinity of GRK2 for the M3R.
source: These results demonstrate, as previously reported (Wolters et al., 2015), that the overexpression of Gq proteins leads to an enhanced affinity of GKR2 for the M3R.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GRK2-mediated phosphorylation of the receptor is initially the rate-limiting step of arrestin binding.
source: Previous studies have shown that GRK2-mediated phosphorylation of the receptor is initially the rate-limiting step of arrestin binding
evidence: This is supported by references to previous studies.

claim: β2-adrenergic receptor-arrestin interaction and M3R-arrestin interaction accelerate with repeated stimulation of the same cell.
source: and that β2-adrenergic receptor-arrestin interaction and M3R-arrestin interaction accelerate with repeated stimulation of the same cell (Krasel et al., 2005; Wolters et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GRK-mediated receptor phosphorylation is in most cases a prerequisite for agonist-evoked arrestin3 binding.
source: Since GRK-mediated receptor phosphorylation is in most cases a prerequisite for agonist-evoked arrestin3 binding (Choi et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Metha-induced arrestin3 recruitment is significantly enhanced after a prepulse with the full agonist ACh.
source: The dependency on agonist-induced phosphorylation for arrestin binding is exemplarily shown in Figure 2C and D as Metha-induced arrestin3 recruitment is significantly enhanced after a prepulse with the full agonist ACh.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The amplitudes measured for prestimulated and not prestimulated M3R differed for all seven agonists except for ACh.
source: The amplitudes measured for prestimulated and not prestimulated M3R differed for all seven agonists except for ACh (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The increase in arrestin3 recruitment amplitude after prestimulation is specific for each agonist, presumably due to differences in their capability to induce phosphorylation of M3R.
source: This indicates that the increase in amplitude after prestimulation is specific for each agonist (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), presumably due to differences in their capability to induce phosphorylation of M3R (Butcher et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, with a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The efficacy ranking of agonists for arrestin3 recruitment to prestimulated M3R is: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Pilo≈Guva>Are>Mda.
source: By applying each of the seven agonists to the M3R subsequent to the prestimulation with ACh, we obtained results that show marked differences in the ability of the individual agonists to recruit arrestin3 to M3R (Figure 2E and F). This led to the following efficacy ranking of the agonists: ACh>Metha≈Fur>Pilo≈Guva>Are>Mda.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The rank order for the efficacy to recruit arrestin3 to M3R differs in comparison to the one obtained for Gq recruitment and activation.
source: It is important to note that the rank order for the efficacy to recruit arrestin3 to M3R differs in comparison to the one obtained for Gq recruitment and activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: The agonist efficacies to recruit Gq to M3R in comparison to D110A-GRK-CAAX were very similar, showing nearly equal efficacy for each agonist.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the agonist efficacies to recruit Gq to M3R in comparison to D110A-GRK-CAAX were very similar, showing nearly equal efficacy for each agonist.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 2D plots comparing agonist efficacies for arrestin3 binding to M3R with those for either Gq or D110A-GRK2-CAAX showed higher relative agonist efficacies for arrestin binding.
source: In contrast, both 2D plots comparing agonist efficacies for arrestin3 binding to M3R with those for either Gq or D110A-GRK2-CAAX showed higher relative agonist efficacies for arrestin binding.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The rank order of agonist efficacies was different for arrestin3 binding as Pilo was more efficient than Are and similarly efficient as Guva to induce arrestin3 recruitment, whereas for both GRK2 recruitment and Gq binding to M3R, Pilo was less efficient than Are and Guva.
source: Most importantly, the rank order of agonist efficacies was different for arrestin3 binding as Pilo was more efficient than Are and similarly efficient as Guva to induce arrestin3 recruitment, whereas for both GRK2 recruitment and Gq binding to M3R, Pilo was less efficient than Are and Guva.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: Agonist efficacies for GRK2 recruitment and Gq activation followed a similar pattern with the identical rank order of agonists.
source: The results confirmed that agonist efficacies for GRK2 recruitment and Gq activation followed a similar pattern with the identical rank order of agonists
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing data using the operational model, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In the case of arrestin3 binding, at least Pilo exhibited a reverted rank order relative to Are and Guva.
source: whereas in the case of arrestin3 binding, at least Pilo exhibited a reverted rank order relative to Are and Guva.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing data using the operational model, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Ligand-induced biased recruitment can be detected at the M3R.
source: Our results show that ligand-induced biased recruitment can indeed be detected at the M3R.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A difference in bias was found between arrestin3 recruitment and the other two effector proteins (Gq and GRK2).
source: Assessing bias as a change in sequence when ranking the agonists with respect to their efficacy to induce Gq, GRK2, or arrestin3 recruitment, we found a difference between arrestin3 recruitment and the other two effector proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: No difference in bias was found between GRK2 recruitment and G protein binding and activation.
source: In contrast, no such difference was found between GRK2 recruitment and G protein binding and activation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Very similar active receptor conformations are required for Gq activation and GRK2 recruitment.
source: suggesting that very similar active receptor conformations are required for Gq activation and GRK2 recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Gq and GRK2 recruitment have the same rank order.

claim: The rank order of agonist efficacies to recruit GRK2 was the same, independent of whether G proteins were inhibited or not.
source: Strikingly, the rank order of agonist efficacies to recruit GRK2 was the same, independent of whether G proteins were inhibited or not.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data under different conditions.

claim: The overall FRET amplitudes and agonist responses normalized to ACh were considerably larger and their overall kinetics considerably slower in the absence of G protein inhibition, demonstrating the contribution of G proteins to translocating GRK2 to the plasma membrane.
source: However, the overall FRET amplitudes and also the agonist responses normalized to the one of ACh were considerably larger and their overall kinetics considerably slower in the absence of G protein inhibition, demonstrating the contribution of G proteins to translocating GRK2 to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data under different conditions.

claim: The rank order of the efficacy of Metha, Are, and Pilo to recruit GRK2 to the M3R is the same as observed for M3R phosphorylation determined by Butcher et al.
source: Importantly, the rank order of the efficacy of Metha, Are, and Pilo to recruit GRK2 to the M3R (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) is the same as observed for M3R phosphorylation determined by Butcher et al. (Figure 6 in Butcher et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature findings, supported by a citation.

claim: GRK2 recruitment to the M3R correlates with functional phosphorylation.
source: indicating that GRK2 recruitment to the M3R correlates with functional phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the current data with previous findings.

claim: Arrestin recruitment to the M3R is dependent on GRK2-mediated phosphorylation.
source: We confirmed arrestin recruitment to the M3R to be dependent on GRK2-mediated phosphorylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: In the absence of coexpression of GRK2 or upon expression of the dominant negative GRK2(K220R), a decrease of the arrestin recruitment was detected.
source: as in the absence of coexpression of GRK2 or upon expression of the dominant negative GRK2(K220R), a decrease of the arrestin recruitment was detected as expected based on previous observations at the β2-adrenergic receptor (Krasel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The dephosphorylation of receptors typically occurs on the order of at least several minutes.
source: As the dephosphorylation of receptors typically occurs on the order of at least several minutes
evidence: This is established knowledge about receptor dephosphorylation kinetics.

claim: The experimental design allowed the comparison of agonist efficacies to prephosphorylated receptors, minimizing any influence of agonist efficacy towards G protein activation and GRK2 binding.
source: our experimental design allowed the comparison of agonist efficacies to prephosphorylated receptors, minimizing any influence of agonist efficacy towards G protein activation and GRK2 binding.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Unlike for G protein and GRK2 recruitment, Pilo induces significantly more arrestin3 recruitment compared to Are.
source: Our results show that unlike for G protein and GRK2 recruitment, Pilo induces significantly more arrestin3 recruitment compared to Are.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The results are in line with a potential bias of Pilo towards arrestin that was reported by Pronin et al., 2017.
source: These results are in line with a potential bias of Pilo towards arrestin that was reported by Pronin et al., 2017.
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The bias towards arrestin recruitment was not introduced by a bias towards GRK2 recruitment.
source: However, here we were able to observe that the bias towards arrestin recruitment was not introduced by a bias towards GRK2 recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: No detectable bias was observed between Gq recruitment and GRK2 recruitment for any of these agonists.
source: In contrast, no detectable bias was observed between Gq recruitment and GRK2 recruitment for any of these agonists.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The findings disentangle bias between Gq, GRK2, and arrestin3 recruitment to the M3R.
source: Our findings disentangle bias between Gq, GRK2, and arrestin3 recruitment to the M3R.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: Arrestin3 recruitment was tested in an overexpression system for all agonists under exactly the same conditions regarding prephosphorylation and kinase expression.
source: Arrestin3 recruitment was tested in an overexpression system for all agonists under exactly the same conditions regarding prephosphorylation and kinase expression.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: The influence of endogenous GRK and arrestin isoforms is negligible in the experimental system used.
source: The influence of endogenous GRK and arrestin isoforms is therefore negligible.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental system based on the overexpression approach.

claim: The overall agonist-dependent recruitment might depend on the expression pattern of GRKs.
source: However, we cannot rule out that the overall agonist-dependent recruitment might as well depend on the expression pattern of GRKs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the findings.

claim: M3R-mediated signaling is regulated by distinct mechanisms.
source: Since M3R-mediated signaling is regulated by distinct mechanisms (Luo et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The results represent the first step on the way to completely disentangle bias signaling.
source: our results represent the first step on the way to completely disentangle bias signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance and limitations of the current findings.

claim: Measurement of agonist-induced G protein recruitment to receptors by means of FRET is a much more direct way to study the efficacy of agonists to activate receptors compared to the measurement of G protein activation or downstream signaling due to its lack of signal amplification.
source: Measurement of agonist-induced G protein recruitment to receptors by means of FRET is a much more direct way to study the efficacy of agonists to activate receptors compared to the measurement of G protein activation or downstream signaling due to its lack of signal amplification, which typically leads to the phenomenon of signal saturation at submaximal levels of receptor activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the FRET-based approach, based on established knowledge.

claim: Metha and Fur recruited arrestin3, GRK2, and Gq to a similar extent compared to the full agonist ACh.
source: Metha and Fur recruited arrestin3, GRK2, and Gq to a similar extent compared to the full agonist ACh
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: The partial agonists Are, Guva, and Pilo differed substantially in their relative efficacy to recruit arrestin3 versus GRK2 and Gq.
source: whereas the partial agonists Are, Guva, and Pilo differed substantially in their relative efficacy to recruit arrestin3 versus GRK2 and Gq (Figures 1B, 2B and F).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data across different assays.

claim: Pilo was the poorest GRK2 and Gq recruiter among the partial agonists, but the best arrestin3 recruiter, indicating a relative bias towards arrestin3 binding.
source: The strongest deviation in the rank order was observed for Pilo, which from the set of partial agonists was the poorest GRK2 and Gq recruiter, but the best arrestin3 recruiter, indicating a relative bias towards arrestin3 binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The slow component of arrestin3 recruitment upon first stimulation with agonist was dependent on the expression of catalytically active GRK2.
source: Even though we did not directly measure GRK2-mediated phosphorylation, we found that the slow component of arrestin3 recruitment upon first stimulation with agonist was dependent on the expression of catalytically active GRK2, similar to what has been described for β2-adrenergic receptors (Krasel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The slow component of arrestin3 recruitment was also visible during subsequent applications of agonist, which could indicate incomplete phosphorylation or reflect phosphorylation-independent effects.
source: However, this slow component, even though it is smaller in amplitude, was also visible during subsequent applications of agonist. This could either indicate incomplete phosphorylation at the time points of the repetitive agonist applications or could reflect phosphorylation-independent effects, such as the interaction of arrestin3 with the membrane and a thus prolonged residence time of arrestin3 at the membrane after the first recruitment to the receptor (Lally et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations, with a citation to support one possible mechanism.

claim: The finding that agonist bias with respect to the ability to activate G proteins versus the ability to induce arrestin recruitment to the receptor can be detected correlates with recent advancements in the determination of conformational differences of the angiotensin-II receptor type 1 when bound to Gq or arrestin.
source: Our finding that agonist bias with respect to the ability to activate G proteins versus the ability to induce arrestin recruitment to the receptor can be detected correlates nicely with recent advancements in the determinnation of conformational differences of the angiotensin-II receptor type 1 when bound to Gq or arrestin (Wingler et al., 2020; Suomivuori et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares the current findings with recent literature, supported by citations.

claim: The results demonstrating the existence of functional agonist-dependent patterns of differential recruitment of arrestin3 and GRK2 to the M3R are supported by a recent study demonstrating agonist-dependent patterns of recruitment of G proteins, GRK2, and a conformationally selective nanobody directed against the intracellular cavity of activated opioid receptors.
